content.thinking: I need to fix that timestamp to the recovered value and drop the vague "about a minute" phrasing, while keeping the three action items numbered correctly as AI-3 through AI-5.

action_items.item: Add a pre-deploy validation step, or a staged rollout with an automatic latency gate, so a revision that makes the service slower is stopped or reverted before it reaches all replicas.
Tighten the latency alert, or add one on a faster-reacting signal, so a sustained latency rise pages close to onset even when the error rate stays flat.
Before merging the proposed fix, read the service logs from the incident window and confirm the mechanism of the slowdown against the diff in the P2 revision. Record the result on the incident.

causal_chain.step: People using io-shop got much slower responses for {duration}. The paging latency series rose from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and peaked at {series_at_worst}. The error rate did not rise above its baseline.
The slowdown began in the same minute as the production deploy of a new revision (P2), and the service was running that revision across its replicas.
The new revision was the cause of the slowdown: rolling the deployment back removed it, the service was back at baseline from {recovered}, and the rule that paged stopped firing.

contributing_factors.factor: The new revision reached every replica without a check that would catch a latency regression, so a slowdown shipped to all traffic.
The alert fired well after onset, {alert_raised - began} later, so users were slowed for that long before anyone responded.
The investigation did not read logs, so the mechanism behind the slowdown is unconfirmed and the proposed fix rests on a hypothesis.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, starting at {began}, pages on the shop were noticeably slower than usual. The latency measure that paged us rose from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and peaked at {series_at_worst}. The share of requests that failed did not rise above its normal level, so the harm was slowness rather than errors. The slowdown began in the same minute as a new release. Argus rolled that release back and the service was back at its baseline by {recovered}. A draft fix has been proposed and is waiting for review. The exact internal mechanism was not confirmed from logs.

got_lucky: The service stayed up and requests kept succeeding while slow. A slowdown of this kind could have turned into timeouts and errors.
went_well: The rollback was started right after the Investigator finished, and the service was confirmed back at baseline before the incident was closed.
The correlation with the deploy change event gave a fast lead candidate, and a draft fix pull request was proposed right after mitigation.
went_wrong: The alert was raised only after the slowdown had already been running for some time.
The Investigator formed its candidates without reading logs, so the mechanism was never confirmed from the record.
The error rate never rose, so users were slowed with nothing in the error metric to show it.

input.root_cause: The revision deployed at P2 slowed the service down from the minute it went out, and rolling it back (M1) restored the baseline. The record does not confirm the exact mechanism: no logs were read, and the suspected cause, a changed cache port in the deploy configuration, is the Investigator's hypothesis only.
